title: Balls into bins
cue: Items distributed among containers: first identify what is distinguishable.
theory: n distinct balls into k distinct bins: kⁿ assignments.
n identical balls into k distinct bins: C(n+k−1,k−1); require every bin nonempty: C(n−1,k−1), when n≥k.
Identical bins change the problem to partitions; ordinary stars and bars does not apply.

recall.q: When is stars and bars valid?
recall.a: Indistinguishable items, distinguishable containers, with integer occupancies and stated bounds.

pitfall: Do not divide by k! automatically when bins are identical; repeated occupancies have different symmetries.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Permutations and combinations
cue: Arrange, choose, distinct digits, balanced parentheses or constrained strings.
theory: Ordered selection of r distinct objects from n: n!/(n−r)!. Unordered selection: C(n,r).
A multiset permutation count is n!/(m₁!m₂!⋯). Balanced parenthesis strings of length 2n are counted by C(2n,n)/(n+1).

recall.q: How do you choose between permutations and combinations?
recall.a: Ask whether exchanging two selected objects creates a different outcome: yes → permutation, no → combination.

pitfall: Leading zero and repeated objects can invalidate a direct n! calculation.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Counting principles
cue: Break the choices into stages, cases, or overlapping sets.
theory: Multiply counts for successive choices when each stage has the stated number of options. Add counts for disjoint alternatives.
card(A∪B)=card(A)+card(B)−card(A∩B). Complement counting often simplifies 'at least one'.

recall.q: Why subtract the intersection in inclusion–exclusion?
recall.a: Outcomes in the intersection were counted once in each set, so one copy must be removed.

pitfall: Add only disjoint case counts, or explicitly compensate for overlaps.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Generating functions
cue: Count ways to achieve a total using allowed contributions.
theory: Represent allowed values for one choice by a polynomial or power series; multiply across choices.
The coefficient of xⁿ in the product counts ways to achieve total n. For nonnegative unrestricted occupancy, use 1+x+x²+⋯.

recall.q: What does the coefficient of x⁷ represent?
recall.a: The number of allowed combinations whose contributions sum to 7, under the model encoded by the factors.

pitfall: A generating function models the allowed values, including upper bounds and whether choices are distinguishable.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Modular arithmetic
cue: Remainders, cyclic patterns or a large exponent's last digits.
theory: a≡b mod m means m divides a−b. Addition and multiplication preserve congruence.
Division by a modulo m is valid only when a has a multiplicative inverse, equivalently gcd(a,m)=1.

recall.q: When can you cancel a factor modulo m?
recall.a: When that factor is invertible modulo m; otherwise cancellation may change the modulus or lose solutions.

pitfall: Do not treat modular division as ordinary integer division.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Pigeonhole principle
cue: A question asks what is guaranteed, regardless of placement.
theory: Putting N objects into k boxes forces at least one box to contain at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects.
To force r objects in one box, (r−1)k+1 objects suffice and are necessary without other constraints.

recall.q: How many objects force 4 into one of 5 boxes?
recall.a: 16, since 15 could be distributed as 3 per box.

pitfall: Choose the boxes carefully: residues, intervals, or possible categories may be the useful bins.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Recurrence relations
cue: A sequence or count is defined from earlier terms.
theory: A recurrence needs initial values as well as a relation. For a homogeneous linear recurrence, try aₙ=rⁿ and solve its characteristic equation.
A repeated characteristic root r of multiplicity s contributes rⁿ times a polynomial in n of degree at most s−1.

recall.q: What extra factor is needed for a repeated root r?
recall.a: Terms rⁿ, nrⁿ, …, nˢ⁻¹rⁿ for multiplicity s.

pitfall: Use all initial conditions; the recurrence alone usually does not determine one sequence.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Finite sums and series
cue: Nested counts, arithmetic growth or a geometric pattern.
theory: For r≠1, 1+r+⋯+rⁿ=(rⁿ⁺¹−1)/(r−1); when r=1 the sum is n+1.

recall.q: How do you check the number of terms in a geometric sum?
recall.a: Count both endpoints: powers 0 through n give n+1 terms.

pitfall: Do not substitute r=1 into a formula with denominator r−1.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Counting graphs
cue: Count possible edges, labelled graphs or spanning trees.
theory: A simple undirected graph on n labelled vertices has C(n,2) possible edges, hence 2^C(n,2) graphs.
The complete labelled graph Kₙ has nⁿ⁻² spanning trees for n≥2.

recall.q: Why is the number of labelled simple graphs 2^C(n,2)?
recall.a: Each possible edge is independently present or absent.

pitfall: Labelled and unlabelled graph counts differ; also check directed versus undirected.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Vertex degree
cue: A degree sequence, edge count, or parity condition appears.
theory: In an undirected graph, Σdeg(v)=2card(E), so the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
In a directed graph, Σindeg(v)=Σoutdeg(v)=card(E). A loop contributes 2 to undirected degree.

recall.q: Is an even degree sum enough to prove a sequence is graphical?
recall.a: No. Other restrictions apply; use a constructive test such as Havel–Hakimi for simple graphs.

pitfall: A parity check can disprove a sequence but cannot by itself prove existence.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Graph algorithms
cue: Connectivity or a traversal is used inside a graph-theory question.
theory: BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing unweighted distance from its source. DFS follows a branch before backtracking.
With adjacency lists, both run in O(V+E); scanning an adjacency matrix requires O(V²).

recall.q: Which traversal gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
recall.a: BFS, with distance counted in edges.

pitfall: Traversal complexity depends on representation, not just the algorithm's name.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Graph colouring
cue: Adjacent vertices must receive different labels or time slots.
theory: A proper vertex colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices; χ(G) is the minimum number needed.
A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle. A bipartite graph with an edge has χ=2; a nonempty edgeless graph has χ=1.

recall.q: What immediately proves a graph is not bipartite?
recall.a: An odd cycle.

pitfall: A matching or independent set is not a colouring; distinguish the object being counted.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Graph connectivity
cue: Paths, bridges, cut vertices, trees, or components appear.
theory: An undirected graph is connected when every pair has a path. A bridge's deletion increases the number of components.
A connected undirected graph with n vertices is a tree iff it has n−1 edges; a tree has a unique simple path between each pair.
Directed strong connectivity requires paths both ways; weak connectivity ignores directions.

recall.q: Can a connected graph with n−1 edges contain a cycle?
recall.a: No; it is a tree.

pitfall: Connectedness and n−1 edges are needed together; an arbitrary n−1-edge graph may be disconnected.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Graph isomorphism
cue: Two drawings may represent the same graph.
theory: An isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. Vertex and edge counts, degree multiset and cycle structure are invariants.
Different invariants disprove isomorphism; matching invariants alone do not prove it.

recall.q: Do equal degree sequences prove two graphs are isomorphic?
recall.a: No. They are a useful necessary check only.

pitfall: Drawing shape and vertex names are irrelevant to isomorphism.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Graph matching
cue: Choose edges with no shared endpoint or pair two sets.
theory: A matching has pairwise vertex-disjoint edges. A maximum matching has largest size; a maximal matching cannot be extended by one edge.
In a bipartite graph, a matching saturating the left side exists iff every subset S on that side has at least card(S) neighbours (Hall's condition).

recall.q: Does maximal imply maximum?
recall.a: No. A locally unextendable matching can be smaller than the largest matching.

pitfall: A perfect matching covers every vertex, so the graph must have an even number of vertices.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Planar graphs
cue: A graph must be drawn without crossing edges, or faces are counted.
theory: For a connected planar embedding, V−E+F=2, counting the unbounded face.
A simple planar graph with V≥3 has E≤3V−6; if it is bipartite, E≤2V−4.

recall.q: Does E≤3V−6 prove planarity?
recall.a: No; it is a necessary condition, not sufficient.

pitfall: The edge bounds assume a simple graph and V≥3.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Jaccard similarity
cue: Compare overlap of sets or neighbourhoods.
theory: J(A,B)=card(A∩B)/card(A∪B) when the union is nonempty.
For vertex similarity, first determine whether the problem uses open or closed neighbourhoods.

recall.q: If two nonempty sets are identical, what is their Jaccard similarity?

pitfall: Do not use intersection divided by the sum of sizes; that double-counts shared elements in the denominator.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: First-order logic
cue: Quantifiers, predicates and statement translations appear.
theory: ¬∀x P(x)≡∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x)≡∀x ¬P(x).
∀x∃y R(x,y) allows y to depend on x; ∃y∀x R(x,y) requires one y to work for all x.
To refute a universal claim, give one counterexample.

recall.q: What is the negation of 'every student solved some question'?
recall.a: 'Some student solved no question', with the same stated domains.

pitfall: Quantifier order generally cannot be swapped.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Logical inference
cue: Decide whether premises force a conclusion.
theory: An argument is valid if no interpretation makes all premises true and its conclusion false.
Modus ponens: P and P→Q imply Q. Modus tollens: ¬Q and P→Q imply ¬P.

recall.q: Does P→Q together with Q imply P?
recall.a: No; that is affirming the consequent.

pitfall: Check validity separately from whether a premise happens to be true in everyday life.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Propositional logic
cue: Truth tables, implication, equivalence or satisfiability appears.
theory: P→Q≡¬P∨Q; it is false only when P is true and Q is false.
A tautology is true for every assignment; satisfiable means true for at least one.
De Morgan: ¬(P∧Q)≡¬P∨¬Q, and ¬(P∨Q)≡¬P∧¬Q.

recall.q: Which statement is equivalent to P→Q: converse or contrapositive?
recall.a: The contrapositive ¬Q→¬P.

pitfall: The converse Q→P and inverse ¬P→¬Q are not generally equivalent to the original implication.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Binary operations
cue: A custom operator is defined on a set.
theory: An operation on S must map every pair in S×S back into S. Test associativity by comparing (a*b)*c and a*(b*c).
An identity e must satisfy e*a=a*e=a for every a; an inverse must work with that identity.

recall.q: What is the first group-axiom check for a custom operation?
recall.a: Closure on the specified set.

pitfall: One numerical example can refute an axiom, but cannot prove it for every input.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Countable and uncountable sets
cue: Compare sizes of infinite sets or sets of sequences.
theory: A countably infinite set admits a bijection with the natural numbers; integers and rationals are countable.
Real numbers and infinite binary sequences are uncountable. Finite strings over a finite alphabet form a countable set.

recall.q: Are all finite binary strings countable?
recall.a: Yes: list them by length and then lexicographically.

pitfall: Infinite strings and arbitrarily long finite strings are different sets.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Functions
cue: Mapping counts, composition, injectivity or surjectivity appears.
theory: A function assigns exactly one codomain value to each domain element. Injective means distinct inputs have distinct outputs; surjective means every codomain element is reached.
From an n-element domain to an m-element codomain there are mⁿ functions.

recall.q: For finite sets, when can an injective function exist?
recall.a: Only when the domain size is no greater than the codomain size.

pitfall: The codomain is declared; the image is the subset actually reached.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Groups and monoids
cue: Identify an algebraic structure from its operation.
theory: A monoid has an associative closed operation and an identity. A group additionally gives every element an inverse; Abelian means commutative.
In a finite group, subgroup order and element order divide group order. Under addition mod n, 0 is the identity.

recall.q: What extra property turns a monoid into a group?
recall.a: Every element must have an inverse within the set.

pitfall: Closure and commutativity alone do not establish a group.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Pointwise operations on functions
cue: An operation on a set of functions is defined by its output at n.
theory: Read the operation's definition: (f⊙g)(n)=f(n)+g(n) is pointwise addition, not composition.
For nonnegative-integer-valued functions, pointwise addition is associative and commutative, with the zero function as identity. Nonzero functions have no additive inverse in this set.

recall.q: Why is this pointwise-addition structure a monoid but not a group?
recall.a: The zero function is an identity, but a nonzero function would need negative values in its inverse.

pitfall: The identity is the zero function here, not the function n↦n.
subject: Engineering Mathematics
