title: Lattices
cue: Find meet, join, complements, or bounds in a Hasse diagram.
theory: A lattice is a partial order in which every pair has a unique greatest lower bound (meet) and least upper bound (join).
In a bounded lattice, b complements a when a∧b=0 and a∨b=1; complements need not be unique or exist.

recall.q: Is every partially ordered set a lattice?
recall.a: No; some pairs may lack a meet or a join.

pitfall: A maximal element need not be the greatest element; bounds must compare with every element in the subset.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Mathematical induction
cue: Prove a statement for every integer from a starting value.
theory: Prove a base case, then show P(k) implies P(k+1). Strong induction may use all earlier cases.
The induction hypothesis is an assumption used to prove the next case, not the conclusion being proved.

recall.q: Why is the base case necessary?
recall.a: It starts the implication chain; the inductive step alone could hold vacuously.

pitfall: Check that the step works at the first index where it is used.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Elementary number theory
cue: Divisibility, gcd, prime factors or integer constraints appears.
theory: The Euclidean algorithm uses gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a mod b). For positive integers, gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b)=ab.
If gcd(a,b)=1 and a divides bc, then a divides c.

recall.q: When can a divisor be cancelled from a product-divisibility claim?
recall.a: Coprimality with the other factor is sufficient.

pitfall: 'a divides bc' alone does not mean a divides b or a divides c.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Surjective functions
cue: Every target value must be hit.
theory: For a finite n-element domain and m-element codomain, surjections require n≥m.
Their count is Σᵢ₌₀ᵐ(−1)ⁱ C(m,i)(m−i)ⁿ, using inclusion–exclusion.

recall.q: Why does counting onto functions need inclusion–exclusion?
recall.a: We exclude functions missing at least one codomain element, correcting overlapping omissions.

pitfall: Do not confuse onto with one-to-one; multiple inputs may map to the same output.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Partial orders
cue: Reflexivity, antisymmetry, transitivity or Hasse diagrams appears.
theory: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. A total order also makes every pair comparable.
Hasse diagrams omit reflexive loops and transitive edges, with larger elements conventionally higher.

recall.q: Can a finite poset have several maximal elements?
recall.a: Yes; they may be incomparable. A greatest element, if present, is unique.

pitfall: Antisymmetry does not mean 'never symmetric'; equality is allowed.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Polynomials
cue: Roots, degree, coefficients or algebraic identities appear.
theory: A nonzero degree-d polynomial over a field has at most d distinct roots.
For ax²+bx+c with a≠0, root sum is −b/a and product is c/a. Equal polynomials have equal corresponding coefficients.

recall.q: How can a polynomial identity valid for all x be converted to equations?
recall.a: Expand and equate coefficients of each power of x.

pitfall: An equation at a few inputs need not be an identity at every input.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Relations
cue: Count or test binary relations, equivalence classes or order properties.
theory: A relation on an n-element set is a subset of A×A, so there are 2^(n²) relations.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive and corresponds to a partition. A partial order uses antisymmetry instead of symmetry.

recall.q: How many reflexive relations exist on an n-element set?
recall.a: 2^(n²−n), since all n diagonal pairs are forced.

pitfall: Symmetric and antisymmetric are separate properties; a relation can satisfy both.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Sets and set algebra
cue: Unions, intersections, complements or power sets appear.
theory: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets. De Morgan gives (A∪B)ᶜ=Aᶜ∩Bᶜ and (A∩B)ᶜ=Aᶜ∪Bᶜ.
card(A×B)=card(A)card(B) for finite sets; A−B=A∩Bᶜ.

recall.q: What is the difference between ∅ and {∅}?
recall.a: The first has zero elements; the second has one element, which is the empty set.

pitfall: Complements depend on the chosen universal set.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Continuity
cue: A piecewise function or a limit at a boundary appears.
theory: Continuity at a requires limₓ→ₐ f(x)=f(a), so both one-sided limits and the assigned value must agree.
Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability.

recall.q: Is abs(x) differentiable at zero?
recall.a: No; it is continuous but its left and right derivatives differ.

pitfall: Checking only the formula on one side misses a discontinuity at a join.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Definite integrals
cue: Compute signed area, a symmetric integral, or an average value.
theory: For continuous f, ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx=F(b)−F(a) when F′=f.
On [−a,a], an odd integrand integrates to 0; an even integrand gives twice the integral on [0,a].

recall.q: Does a definite integral always equal geometric area?
recall.a: No; portions below the axis contribute negative signed area.

pitfall: Reversing integration limits reverses the sign.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Differentiation
cue: Find a slope, derivative, tangent or rate of change.
theory: Use the chain rule: d[f(g(x))]/dx=f′(g(x))g′(x). Product rule: (uv)′=u′v+uv′.
At an interior differentiable local extremum, f′=0, but a stationary point need not be an extremum.
Mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some c in (a,b) satisfies f′(c)=[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a).

recall.q: Why is f′(a)=0 not enough to prove an extremum?
recall.a: A stationary inflection point such as x³ at zero also has derivative zero.

pitfall: Do not forget the derivative of the inner function.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Integration
cue: Find an antiderivative or transform an integral.
theory: Substitution reverses the chain rule; integration by parts uses ∫u dv=uv−∫v du.
An indefinite integral includes an arbitrary constant. For a definite integral, change bounds when substituting variables.

recall.q: What does ' + C' represent?
recall.a: All antiderivatives differing by a constant on the interval.

pitfall: The antiderivative of 1/x is ln(abs(x)) on an interval not crossing zero.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Limits
cue: Behaviour near a point, infinity, or an indeterminate form appears.
theory: A two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and agree.
Factor, rationalize, or use a standard limit before direct substitution into 0/0.
limₓ→₀ sin(x)/x=1 when angles are in radians.

recall.q: What does the expression 0/0 tell you about a limit?
recall.a: Only that the form is indeterminate; further analysis is needed.

pitfall: The function's value at the point need not equal, or even exist with, its limit.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Maxima and minima
cue: Optimize a function on an interval or under a constraint.
theory: For a continuous function on a closed bounded interval, compare all interior critical points and both endpoints.
f″(a)>0 at a stationary point gives a local minimum; f″(a)<0 gives a local maximum. f″(a)=0 is inconclusive.

recall.q: Where can an absolute extremum on [a,b] occur?
recall.a: At an endpoint or an interior critical point, including points where the derivative is undefined.

pitfall: A local optimum need not be the global optimum.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Polynomial behaviour
cue: Polynomial roots, derivatives or shape is used in calculus.
theory: A degree-d polynomial has a derivative of degree d−1 when d≥1.
Between two distinct real zeros of a differentiable polynomial lies a zero of its derivative (Rolle's theorem).

recall.q: What does Rolle's theorem require on [a,b]?
recall.a: Continuity on [a,b], differentiability on (a,b), and equal endpoint values.

pitfall: Rolle's theorem guarantees existence, not a unique stationary point.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Series and telescoping sums
cue: A sum contains differences of neighbouring terms.
theory: Rewrite aₖ=bₖ−bₖ₊₁ so internal terms cancel and only boundary terms remain.
For infinite series, examine partial sums and their limit; finite-sum identities alone do not establish convergence.

recall.q: What is Σₖ₌₁ⁿ[1/k−1/(k+1)]?

pitfall: Write a few beginning and ending terms to avoid losing an endpoint.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Coordinate vectors
cue: Lengths, projections or coordinates appear in linear algebra.
theory: In Euclidean coordinates, u·v=Σuᵢvᵢ and norm(u)=√(u·u).
The distance between points p and q is norm(p−q).

recall.q: How do you test whether two nonzero vectors are perpendicular?
recall.a: Their dot product is zero.

pitfall: A vector's coordinates depend on the basis; geometric length uses the stated inner product.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Determinants
cue: Invertibility, volume scaling or determinant operations appear.
theory: det(AB)=det(A)det(B), and det(Aᵀ)=det(A). A square matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero.
Swapping rows negates the determinant; multiplying one row by c scales it by c; adding a multiple of another row leaves it unchanged.

recall.q: For n×n A, what is det(cA)?
recall.a: cⁿ det(A).

pitfall: Scaling every row differs from scaling just one row.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
cue: Av=λv or powers of a matrix appear.
theory: An eigenvector v must be nonzero. Eigenvalues solve det(A−λI)=0.
Eigenvalue sum equals trace and product equals determinant, counting algebraic multiplicity. Eigenvalues of Aᵏ are λᵏ.

recall.q: Can the zero vector be an eigenvector?
recall.a: No, otherwise Av=λv would hold trivially for every λ.

pitfall: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors need not be real for a real matrix.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Gaussian elimination
cue: Solve equations or compute matrix rank using row operations.
theory: Elementary row operations preserve the solution set of an augmented system. Echelon form reveals pivots and free variables.
A row [0 … 0 : c] with c≠0 makes the system inconsistent.

recall.q: What does a pivot column represent in a linear system?
recall.a: A basic variable; nonpivot columns correspond to free variables in a consistent system.

pitfall: When solving Ax=b, apply row operations to the entire augmented matrix, including b.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: LU decomposition
cue: Factor a matrix to solve several linear systems efficiently.
theory: LU expresses A as a lower-triangular matrix times an upper-triangular matrix when the needed elimination pivots are available.
With row pivoting, the relation is PA=LU. Solve Ly=Pb, then Ux=y.

recall.q: Why does a permutation matrix appear in PA=LU?
recall.a: It records row swaps used to obtain suitable pivots.

pitfall: A zero pivot can require row permutation even when A is invertible.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Matrix operations
cue: Dimensions, matrix products, inverses or special matrices appear.
theory: If A is m×n and B is n×p, AB is m×p. Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.
For invertible square matrices, (AB)⁻¹=B⁻¹A⁻¹; also (AB)ᵀ=BᵀAᵀ.

recall.q: What order do factors take when a product is inverted?
recall.a: Reverse order.

pitfall: AB may exist when BA does not, or they may have different dimensions.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Eigenvalue multiplicity
cue: Repeated eigenvalues or diagonalizability appears.
theory: Algebraic multiplicity counts a root's multiplicity in the characteristic polynomial; geometric multiplicity is dim ker(A−λI).
Over a field where the characteristic polynomial splits, diagonalizability requires geometric and algebraic multiplicities to agree for every eigenvalue.

recall.q: Do repeated eigenvalues prevent diagonalization?
recall.a: No; enough linearly independent eigenvectors may still exist.

pitfall: Check the field: a real matrix may diagonalize over complex numbers but not over the reals.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Orthonormal vectors
cue: Orthogonal bases, projections or length preservation appears.
theory: Orthonormal vectors are mutually perpendicular and each has unit length. For real square Q with orthonormal columns, QᵀQ=I and Q⁻¹=Qᵀ.
Projection onto a unit vector u is (uᵀv)u.

recall.q: What additional condition distinguishes orthonormal from orthogonal?
recall.a: Every vector must have norm 1.

pitfall: Normalize after Gram–Schmidt; perpendicular vectors are not automatically unit vectors.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Matrix rank
cue: Linear independence, nullity or consistency appears.
theory: Rank is the number of pivots, equal to both row rank and column rank. For m×n A, rank(A)+nullity(A)=n.
Ax=b is consistent iff rank(A)=rank([A : b]); it has a unique solution iff this rank equals n.

recall.q: Which dimension appears in rank-nullity: rows or columns?
recall.a: The number of columns, which is the dimension of the input space.

pitfall: Use the augmented matrix to test consistency, not rank(A) alone.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Singular value decomposition
cue: A matrix is factored using orthogonal matrices, or singular values appear.
theory: For a real m×n matrix, A=UΣVᵀ with U,V orthogonal and Σ diagonal-shaped with nonnegative entries.
Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA; the number of positive singular values equals rank(A).

recall.q: Can a rectangular matrix have an SVD?
recall.a: Yes.

pitfall: Singular values are nonnegative; they are not generally the eigenvalues of A.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Statistics with vectors
cue: Mean-centred data, covariance or linear transformations appear.
theory: The mean of x₁,…,xₙ is (Σxᵢ)/n. Centering subtracts that mean from every observation.
For covariance, centre each variable before multiplying deviations; population and sample conventions use different divisors.

recall.q: What is the sum of deviations from the arithmetic mean?
recall.a: Zero.

pitfall: Do not silently interchange division by n and by n−1.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Subspaces
cue: A set of vectors must be tested for closure.
theory: A nonempty subset is a subspace if it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. It must contain the zero vector.
A homogeneous linear system Ax=0 defines a subspace; Ax=b with b≠0 does not.

recall.q: What is a quick way to disprove that a set is a subspace?
recall.a: Show it does not contain the zero vector.

pitfall: Containing zero is necessary, but not sufficient.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Systems of linear equations
cue: Classify solutions as none, one or infinitely many.
theory: For n unknowns, compare rank(A) and rank([A : b]). Unequal ranks mean no solution; equal rank n means a unique solution.
Equal rank r<n gives n−r free parameters over the reals or complexes.

recall.q: Can a homogeneous system be inconsistent?
recall.a: No; the zero solution always exists.

pitfall: A singular coefficient matrix does not by itself mean no solution.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Vector spaces and bases
cue: Spanning sets, basis, dimension or dependence appears.
theory: A basis is a linearly independent spanning set; all bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same size.
In an n-dimensional space, more than n vectors are dependent; n independent vectors form a basis.

recall.q: Are n spanning vectors in an n-dimensional space a basis?
recall.a: Yes.

pitfall: A spanning set can contain redundant vectors and need not be a basis.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Bayes' theorem
cue: Reverse a conditional probability after observing evidence.
theory: P(A given B)=P(B given A)P(A)/P(B), provided P(B)>0.
For a partition Aᵢ, P(B)=ΣP(B given Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ); these terms supply the denominator.

recall.q: What are the numerator's two factors in Bayes' theorem?
recall.a: Likelihood of evidence under the hypothesis times the prior probability of that hypothesis.

pitfall: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are generally different.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Bayesian networks
cue: A directed acyclic probability graph or conditional independence appears.
theory: A Bayesian network factorizes a joint distribution as ∏P(Xᵢ given parents(Xᵢ)).
Conditional independence is assessed from the graph's path rules and what is observed; it cannot be read from missing arrows alone without care.

recall.q: How is the joint distribution factorized in a Bayesian network?
recall.a: Multiply each node's conditional probability given its parents.

pitfall: Conditioning on a collider or its descendant can create dependence along a previously blocked path.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Bernoulli distribution
cue: One success/failure trial is encoded by 1 and 0.
theory: If X is Bernoulli(p), P(X=1)=p and P(X=0)=1−p.
E[X]=p and Var(X)=p(1−p), because X²=X.

recall.q: Why does E[X²]=p for a Bernoulli variable?
recall.a: Its only values are 0 and 1, so X²=X.

pitfall: The probability p refers to the outcome designated as success, not necessarily heads or winning.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Binomial distribution
cue: Count successes in a fixed number of independent equal-probability trials.
theory: For X∼Binomial(n,p), P(X=k)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. E[X]=np and Var(X)=np(1−p).
Drawing without replacement from a finite population is generally hypergeometric, not binomial.

recall.q: What three cues suggest a binomial count?
recall.a: Fixed n, independent trials, and the same success probability p on each trial.

pitfall: 'Exactly k' differs from 'at least k'; the latter is a sum or a complement.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Chi-square distribution
cue: Sum of squared independent standard normal variables appears.
theory: If Z₁,…,Zₖ are independent standard normal variables, ΣZᵢ² has a chi-square distribution with k degrees of freedom.
Its mean is k and variance is 2k.

recall.q: What assumptions are needed before summing squared normals gives χ²ₖ?
recall.a: The variables must be independent and standard normal.

pitfall: Squaring arbitrary normal variables does not automatically give a standard chi-square law.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Conditional probability
cue: The phrase 'given that' restricts the sample space.
theory: P(A given B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. In equally likely finite outcomes, count favourable outcomes within B.
Sampling without replacement changes the later draw probabilities.

recall.q: If the older of two children is a girl, what outcomes remain under independent equal-likelihood sexes?
recall.a: GG and GB, so the probability of two girls is 1/2.

pitfall: 'Older is a girl' and 'at least one is a girl' condition on different events.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Continuous random variables
cue: A probability is found from area under a density.
theory: A continuous variable has P(a≤X≤b)=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx and P(X=x)=0 at any single point.
Its CDF is F(x)=P(X≤x); where differentiable, F′=f.

recall.q: Can a density value f(x) exceed 1?
recall.a: Yes; only total area must equal 1.

pitfall: Density height is not the probability at that exact point.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Expectation
cue: Find an average payoff, count, or transformed variable.
theory: E[g(X)]=Σg(x)P(X=x) for discrete X, or the corresponding density integral.
Linearity E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c does not require independence. Indicator variables often simplify counts.

recall.q: Does linearity of expectation require independence?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: E[g(X)] is generally not g(E[X]).
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Exponential distribution
cue: Waiting time for a constant-rate event or memorylessness appears.
theory: For rate λ>0, f(x)=λ exp(−λx) for x≥0 and P(X>t)=exp(−λt).
Mean is 1/λ and variance is 1/λ². Memorylessness: P(X>s+t given X>s)=P(X>t).

recall.q: If rate doubles, what happens to mean waiting time?
recall.a: It halves.

pitfall: Check whether the question parameterizes by rate λ or scale 1/λ.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Independent events
cue: An event's probability is unchanged by knowing another occurred.
theory: A and B are independent iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
Pairwise independence among several events does not generally imply mutual independence.

recall.q: Can disjoint positive-probability events be independent?
recall.a: No: their intersection has probability 0 but the product of probabilities is positive.

pitfall: Disjoint means cannot occur together; independent means no probability information about each other.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Normal distribution
cue: A bell-shaped continuous variable, z-score or standard normal appears.
theory: If X∼N(μ,σ²) with σ>0, Z=(X−μ)/σ is standard normal.
Symmetry gives P(Z≤−z)=P(Z≥z); mean and median are μ.

recall.q: When standardizing, divide by variance or standard deviation?
recall.a: Standard deviation σ.

pitfall: In N(μ,σ²), the second parameter is commonly the variance; read the stated convention.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Poisson distribution
cue: Count events in a fixed interval with a constant average event rate.
theory: For X∼Poisson(λ), P(X=k)=exp(−λ)λᵏ/k!, k=0,1,…; E[X]=Var(X)=λ.
Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson variable with the sum of their parameters.

recall.q: If the mean rate is r per hour, what λ is used for t hours?
recall.a: λ=rt.

pitfall: Do not use the per-hour parameter unchanged for a different interval length.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Basic probability and sampling
cue: Equally likely outcomes, complements, dice, coins or random selections appear.
theory: For equally likely finite outcomes, probability is favourable count divided by total count. P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A).
Without replacement, selecting k successes among n draws uses C(K,k)C(N−K,n−k)/C(N,n).

recall.q: Why use combinations for an unordered draw without replacement?
recall.a: Each selected set is one outcome, regardless of drawing order.

pitfall: A favourable-over-total ratio is valid only when the counted elementary outcomes are equally likely.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Probability density functions
cue: Normalize a density or integrate over an interval.
theory: A valid density is nonnegative and integrates to 1 over its support.
Interval probabilities are integrals of the density; points have probability zero for a continuous variable.

recall.q: How do you find a missing normalizing constant c?
recall.a: Set the integral of the density over its support equal to 1.

pitfall: Integrate only where the density is defined as nonzero.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Probability distributions
cue: A probability table, PMF or CDF describes all possible values.
theory: A PMF gives P(X=x) and sums to 1. A CDF gives P(X≤x), is nondecreasing and right-continuous.
A jump in a CDF at x equals P(X=x).

recall.q: How do you recover a point mass from a CDF?

pitfall: A CDF is right-continuous, not necessarily continuous or left-continuous.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Random variables
cue: Turn random outcomes into numerical values.
theory: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome; different outcomes can map to the same value.
For Y=g(X), combine probabilities of all X values yielding the same Y.
Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]; independence implies zero covariance when moments exist.

recall.q: If several outcomes produce X=2, how is P(X=2) found?
recall.a: Add the probabilities of all those outcomes.

pitfall: Zero covariance alone does not generally imply independence.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Polynomial invariance and probability
cue: A question defines a custom property and then samples objects satisfying it.
theory: Use the definition in the question: here the multiset of roots {α,β} equals {α²,β²}.
Split into roots fixed individually and roots exchanged by squaring; identify distinct polynomials before counting favourable ones.
Equal polynomials can be checked by matching coefficients.

recall.q: Why is this not a chi-square or variance problem?
recall.a: 'Square invariant' is explicitly defined for polynomial roots in the PYQ; it does not name a probability distribution.

pitfall: Count distinct polynomials, not ordered root pairs; swapping roots leaves the polynomial unchanged.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

correction.original: The note speculates that Square Invariant concerns squared random variables, variance or chi-square distributions.
correction.corrected: The PYQ on page 223 explicitly defines square-invariant quadratic polynomials through their roots. Solve the algebraic invariance condition, count distinct polynomials, then compute probability.
correction.reason: The source note is about a different concept than the source question.

title: Descriptive statistics
cue: Mean, median, mode or spread is requested.
theory: Mean is the arithmetic average; median is the middle of sorted data (average of the two middle values for even size); mode is a most frequent value.
Population variance averages squared deviations using n; unbiased sample variance uses n−1 under the standard sampling assumptions.

recall.q: Which measure of centre is less sensitive to an extreme outlier: mean or median?
recall.a: Median.

pitfall: Sort the data before finding the median; a dataset may have multiple modes.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Uniform distribution
cue: All values in a range or a finite set are equally likely.
theory: For continuous Uniform(a,b), density is 1/(b−a), mean (a+b)/2 and variance (b−a)²/12.
A subinterval probability is its length divided by b−a, after intersecting with [a,b].

recall.q: For Uniform(2,8), what is P(3≤X≤5)?

pitfall: Continuous interval lengths differ from counts of integers in an inclusive range.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Variance and covariance
cue: Measure spread or the variability of a sum or scaling.
theory: Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]² and Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X).
Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y); independence makes the covariance term zero when moments exist.

recall.q: Does adding a constant change variance?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Variances add for uncorrelated variables, not automatically for every pair.
subject: Engineering Mathematics

title: Age relationships
cue: Translate present, past and future ages into equations.
theory: If present age is x, age t years later is x+t and t years earlier is x−t.
Age differences remain constant over time; age ratios generally change.

recall.q: Which remains constant as two people age: their age difference or ratio?
recall.a: Their age difference.

pitfall: Apply a time shift to every person's age in the statement, not just one.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Analogies
cue: A pair or pattern defines a relationship to reproduce.
theory: Name the relationship in a precise sentence: part-to-whole, function, cause, category, or degree.
Preserve both the relation and its direction when selecting the matching pair.

recall.q: What should be matched in an analogy?
recall.a: The relation between the terms, rather than a vague similarity of the terms themselves.

pitfall: A reversed relation may use plausible words but still be wrong.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Code words
cue: Infer mappings from several coded phrases.
theory: Compare messages that share exactly one concept to isolate its code, then use elimination.
Keep multiple candidates when the evidence does not determine a unique mapping.

recall.q: When can one common code be assigned to one common word?
recall.a: When the compared statements and coding rules rule out other shared mappings.

pitfall: Do not assume word order is preserved unless the coding rule says so.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Coding and decoding
cue: Letters or numbers are transformed by a repeatable rule.
theory: Write letter positions (A=1 through Z=26) and test shifts, reversal, alternation or position-dependent rules.
Check a candidate rule against every supplied example before applying it.

recall.q: How should a letter shift past Z be handled?
recall.a: Wrap cyclically through the alphabet, if that is the stated or established rule.

pitfall: A rule fitting one example may fail the others.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Direction sense
cue: Movement, turns or final displacement appears.
theory: Choose coordinates: east +x, north +y. Add displacements component by component.
Distance travelled is the sum of path lengths; straight-line displacement is √(Δx²+Δy²).

recall.q: If you walk 3 east and 4 north, what is displacement magnitude?

pitfall: Left and right are relative to the current heading, not a fixed compass direction.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Family relationships
cue: Resolve kinship from several relationship statements.
theory: Draw a small family tree and label generations and only explicitly known genders.
Work one relationship at a time, keeping the person speaking as the reference point.

recall.q: Should a name alone determine a person's gender in a logic puzzle?
recall.a: No; use the stated relationship or explicit information.

pitfall: Do not assume unstated family structure or gender.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Necessary inferences
cue: A conclusion must follow from stated facts.
theory: Accept only what is forced in every situation satisfying the premises.
To disprove a proposed inference, construct one situation where the premises hold and the conclusion fails.

recall.q: What is enough to show an inference is not necessary?
recall.a: One valid counterexample.

pitfall: A plausible or likely conclusion is not necessarily a logical consequence.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Constraint-based reasoning
cue: Several clues restrict possible assignments or arrangements.
theory: Represent entities in a table or diagram, place the strongest constraints first, and eliminate contradictions.
When several possibilities remain, test the requested property across all of them.

recall.q: What proves an arrangement is impossible?
recall.a: It violates at least one required constraint.

pitfall: Do not stop after finding one valid arrangement if the question asks what must always hold.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Number relationships
cue: Find a numerical rule relating given values.
theory: Try simple arithmetic, ratios, differences and digit operations, and check the same rule on every example.
If several rules fit, use the answer choices and explicit constraints to discriminate.

recall.q: Why test a pattern on all supplied pairs?
recall.a: A coincidental fit to one pair is weak evidence.

pitfall: Avoid an unnecessarily complicated rule when a consistent simpler one fits.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Odd one out
cue: Identify the option breaking a common property.
theory: Look for one shared structural property among all but one option: category, parity, factor pattern or transformation.
State the property explicitly before selecting the exception.

recall.q: What makes an odd-one-out explanation useful?
recall.a: It identifies a clear property shared by the other options.

pitfall: A superficial difference may not be the intended structural distinction.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Reading for inference
cue: A passage is followed by a statement or conclusion.
theory: Separate what the passage states from what it merely suggests.
Use the author's evidence and scope; eliminate choices that strengthen a claim beyond the text.

recall.q: Can outside knowledge justify a passage answer unsupported by the passage?
recall.a: No; answer from the supplied text.

pitfall: Watch absolute words such as all, never and only when the passage is qualified.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Circular arrangements
cue: People sit around a circular table.
theory: For n distinct people around an unlabelled circle, rotations are identical and the count is (n−1)!.
Fix one person to remove rotational symmetry; treat reflections as distinct unless specified otherwise.

recall.q: Why do circular arrangements use (n−1)! rather than n!?
recall.a: The n rotations of each ordering represent the same circular arrangement.

pitfall: Facing inward versus outward reverses left/right relations.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Seating arrangements
cue: Position people in a row or circle with neighbour constraints.
theory: Translate 'next to', 'between', 'left of' and 'opposite' into positional restrictions.
For a row, label positions; for a circle, fix an anchor and track the facing direction.

recall.q: Does 'to the left of' always mean immediately next to?
recall.a: No; immediate adjacency must be stated.

pitfall: Distinguish a person's own left from the diagram's left.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Sequence patterns
cue: Infer missing terms from a numerical or symbolic sequence.
theory: Check first differences, second differences, ratios, alternating subsequences and simple recurrences.
Verify the proposed rule on every known transition.

recall.q: When are second differences a useful clue?
recall.a: When first differences change by a constant amount, suggesting quadratic growth.

pitfall: A short finite sequence can fit many rules; respect all given constraints.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Statements and conclusions
cue: Choose which conclusions logically follow.
theory: Translate each statement into a precise set or implication relationship, then test the conclusion.
'All A are B' means A is a subset of B; it does not by itself say every B is A.

recall.q: Does 'all roses are flowers' imply 'all flowers are roses'?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Do not assume existence from a universal statement unless the question's logic convention supplies it.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Investment arithmetic
cue: Number of shares, purchase cost and sale value appears.
theory: Units purchased = amount invested ÷ purchase price per unit.
Total profit = sum of sale proceeds − sum of original investments.

recall.q: What must be calculated before finding sale proceeds for each stock?
recall.a: How many units were purchased.

pitfall: A percentage price change must be weighted by the amount invested, not averaged blindly.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Absolute values
cue: Expressions contain distances from zero or piecewise signs.
theory: For x≥0, abs(x)=x; for x<0, abs(x)=−x. Interpret abs(x−a) as distance from a.
Solve by splitting the number line at values where the expressions inside absolute signs change sign.

recall.q: How is abs(x−3)≤2 interpreted?
recall.a: The distance from 3 is at most 2, so 1≤x≤5.

pitfall: Do not remove absolute-value signs without checking the sign inside.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Algebraic translation
cue: A word problem describes unknown quantities and relationships.
theory: Choose variables with clear meanings, write each relationship as an equation, then substitute the result back.
Preserve equality by performing the same operation on both sides.

recall.q: Why check the final values in the original wording?
recall.a: Algebra can introduce extraneous solutions or misrepresent a condition.

pitfall: Dividing by an expression assumes it is nonzero.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Mixtures and weighted averages
cue: Combine substances with different concentrations or prices.
theory: Total amount of solute or cost is additive; final concentration is total solute divided by total volume under the stated model.
For concentrations a<c<b, amounts in the ratio (b−c):(c−a) give concentration c.

recall.q: Why is the mixture concentration between the two original concentrations?
recall.a: It is a weighted average with nonnegative weights.

pitfall: Percentages need weighting by amounts; their simple average works only for equal amounts.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Area
cue: Find the size of a two-dimensional region.
theory: Rectangle area is length×width; triangle area is base×perpendicular height/2.
Scaling all lengths by k scales area by k².

recall.q: If side lengths double, how does area change?
recall.a: It becomes four times as large.

pitfall: Use perpendicular height, not a slanted side, in a triangle area formula.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Arithmetic progressions
cue: Consecutive terms differ by a constant.
theory: The nth term is a+(n−1)d. The sum of n terms is n[2a+(n−1)d]/2.
Equally spaced terms have mean equal to the average of the first and last terms.

recall.q: How many gaps separate the first and nth term?

pitfall: Do not confuse the term number with the number of common-difference steps.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Averages
cue: Combine group means or recover a missing value.
theory: Mean = total ÷ count, so total = count×mean.
Combined mean = (n₁m₁+n₂m₂)/(n₁+n₂).

recall.q: When is the average of two group means their combined mean?
recall.a: When the groups have equal size, or by coincidence their means agree.

pitfall: Weight means by group size.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Bar charts
cue: Compare categories represented by bar heights.
theory: Read axes, scale, units and the baseline before comparing bars.
Compute a percentage change using the original category value as denominator.

recall.q: What denominator is used for increase from 40 to 50?
recall.a: 40, giving 25%.

pitfall: A truncated vertical axis can exaggerate visual differences.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Bayes in aptitude
cue: Reverse a conditional using group proportions and observed evidence.
theory: Count each group's contribution to the observed event, then divide the target group's contribution by the total.
P(cause given evidence) is proportional to prior probability×likelihood.

recall.q: Why do base rates matter in Bayes problems?
recall.a: A rare group can contribute few observed cases even when its conditional rate is high.

pitfall: Do not use a test's accuracy as the posterior probability without accounting for prevalence.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Coordinate geometry
cue: Locations, slopes or distances are given as coordinates.
theory: Distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²].
Midpoint is ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2); slope is Δy/Δx when Δx≠0.

recall.q: What is the slope of a vertical line?
recall.a: Undefined.

pitfall: A line's slope formula cannot be used by dividing by zero.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Circles
cue: Radius, circumference, chords or sectors appear.
theory: Circumference is 2πr and area is πr². For central angle θ in radians, arc length is rθ and sector area is r²θ/2.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.

recall.q: If radius triples, how does circle area change?
recall.a: It multiplies by 9.

pitfall: Do not insert degrees into a formula that assumes radians.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Clock angles
cue: Find the angle between clock hands or coincidence times.
theory: The minute hand moves 6° per minute; the hour hand moves 0.5° per minute.
At h:m, their angular positions from 12 are 30h+0.5m and 6m degrees.

recall.q: What is the relative angular speed of the two hands?
recall.a: 5.5° per minute.

pitfall: The hour hand moves continuously during the hour.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Counting selections and arrangements
cue: Choose or arrange objects under restrictions.
theory: Use nPr for ordered choices and nCr for unordered choices without repetition.
Enforce restrictions before counting; a block method can handle objects required to stay together.

recall.q: If two people must sit together in a row, what is a useful first step?
recall.a: Treat them as one block, then count their internal orders.

pitfall: Do not forget internal permutations within a block.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Compound interest
cue: A balance grows by a repeated proportional rate.
theory: After n equal compounding periods at rate r per period, A=P(1+r)ⁿ.
With m compounding periods per year and nominal annual rate R, use R/m per period and mt periods over t years.

recall.q: What changes when interest compounds quarterly?
recall.a: The rate per period and the number of periods both change.

pitfall: Use a decimal rate and match its time unit to the number of periods.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Conditional sampling
cue: Information restricts the possible outcomes of a random experiment.
theory: P(A given B)=P(A and B)/P(B), for P(B)>0.
For equally likely outcomes, count within the restricted event B.

recall.q: What is the new sample space after conditioning on B?
recall.a: Only outcomes in B.

pitfall: Do not retain the original denominator after restricting to the given event.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Contour plots
cue: Equal-value curves depict a quantity over a plane.
theory: Each contour connects locations sharing the same plotted value.
A steeper change corresponds to closer contours only when their value intervals are comparable.

recall.q: What should be checked before inferring steepness from contour spacing?
recall.a: The contour-value interval and axis scales.

pitfall: Closely drawn curves with unequal value steps need not imply the same gradient.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Cost, marked price and discounts
cue: Cost price, listed price, selling price or a discount appears.
theory: Profit = selling price−cost price; profit percentage uses cost price as denominator.
Selling price after discount d is marked price×(1−d), with d a decimal fraction.

recall.q: Is a 20% discount necessarily a 20% loss?
recall.a: No; discount is measured from marked price, loss from cost price.

pitfall: Keep cost, marked and selling prices separate.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Cubes and painted solids
cue: A cube is cut into equal smaller cubes or faces are painted.
theory: For an n×n×n subdivision of a cube with all outer faces painted and n≥2: 8 corner cubes have 3 painted faces.
For n≥3, 12(n−2) edge-interior cubes have 2 painted faces and 6(n−2)² face-interior cubes have 1.

recall.q: How many completely unpainted small cubes are inside for n≥2?

pitfall: These counts assume every outer face is painted and a uniform cubic grid.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Currency denominations
cue: Count banknotes or represent a total value.
theory: Let each denomination's count be a nonnegative integer; write one equation for value and another for total count if given.
Divisibility and remainder constraints can eliminate impossible counts quickly.

recall.q: Why must denomination variables be integers?
recall.a: They count individual notes or coins.

pitfall: A real-valued algebraic solution may not correspond to a possible set of notes.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Data interpretation
cue: Extract comparisons or implications from a chart, table or described trend.
theory: Identify the quantity being compared and its units before calculating.
Separate absolute change, relative change and rate of change; they answer different questions.

recall.q: Can a larger percentage increase correspond to a smaller absolute increase?
recall.a: Yes, if it starts from a smaller base.

pitfall: A trend or correlation does not alone establish a cause.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Counting pixels from a grid
cue: A displayed array of pixel values is tested against a threshold.
theory: Treat the image as a table of numbers and count entries satisfying the stated inequality.
Keep strict and inclusive bounds distinct, such as I>k versus I≥k.

recall.q: Does a pixel exactly equal to k count when the condition is I>k?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: This PYQ needs careful counting, not advanced image-processing theory.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Factors and divisibility
cue: Count multiples, divisors or integers excluded by a divisibility rule.
theory: Multiples of d in [L,U] number ⌊U/d⌋−⌊(L−1)/d⌋ for positive integer bounds.
If n=∏pᵢ^aᵢ, its number of positive divisors is ∏(aᵢ+1).

recall.q: Why does exponent a contribute a+1 choices to a divisor?
recall.a: The divisor may use that prime with exponent 0 through a.

pitfall: Inclusive interval endpoints affect a count of multiples.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Fractions and ratios
cue: A whole is split into parts or equal fractions of parts are given.
theory: Use a common denominator for addition and subtraction. If x/3=y/2, cross multiplication gives 2x=3y and x:y=3:2.
If x+y=T, this ratio gives x=3T/5 and y=2T/5.

recall.q: Why is the first part 3/5 of the total when x:y=3:2?
recall.a: The total is 5 equal ratio units, and x contains 3 of them.

pitfall: The denominators in equal fractions do not give the same-order fractions of the total without solving the ratio.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Functions in aptitude
cue: Inputs are mapped to outputs using a rule or graph.
theory: A function gives exactly one output for each permitted input.
Composition f(g(x)) applies g first; solve domain restrictions before substituting.

recall.q: In f(g(x)), which function is evaluated first?
recall.a: g.

pitfall: A formula can be undefined for some inputs, such as a zero denominator or an invalid real square root.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Geometry
cue: Angles, distances, parallel lines or similar shapes appear.
theory: Triangle interior angles sum to 180° in Euclidean geometry.
Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths; area ratios are squared length ratios.

recall.q: If similar triangles have side ratio 2:3, what is their area ratio?

pitfall: Similarity does not imply equal size; congruence does.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Colouring constraints
cue: Assign labels so connected or adjacent objects differ.
theory: Model objects as vertices and conflicts as edges; adjacent vertices must have different colours.
A triangle needs 3 colours; an even cycle needs 2 and an odd cycle needs 3.

recall.q: Why can a triangle not be coloured with two colours?
recall.a: All three pairs of vertices are adjacent.

pitfall: Use the actual adjacency relation, not visual closeness in a drawing.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Line charts
cue: Compare values or trends across an ordered axis.
theory: Read each point from the axes and identify whether the horizontal intervals are equal.
Slope is change in vertical quantity divided by change in horizontal quantity.

recall.q: Does a steeper drawn line always mean faster real growth?
recall.a: Only if axes and their scales are comparable.

pitfall: A rising value may have a falling growth rate.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Logarithms
cue: An unknown occurs in an exponent or logarithmic expression.
theory: log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y and log_b(xᵏ)=k log_b x for positive x,y and valid base b>0, b≠1.
Change of base: log_b x=ln x/ln b.

recall.q: Is log(x+y)=log x+log y?
recall.a: No; the product rule applies to xy, not x+y.

pitfall: Real logarithms require positive arguments.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Maps and routes
cue: Convert map lengths to real distances or follow a route.
theory: Apply the stated scale consistently and convert units before combining distances.
Track directions separately from lengths; a map route may be longer than straight-line displacement.

recall.q: At scale 1:50,000, what real distance is 1 cm?

pitfall: Do not compare centimetres on a map directly with kilometres on the ground.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Optimization in aptitude
cue: Find the greatest or least feasible value.
theory: List constraints before optimizing. A quadratic ax²+bx+c has vertex at x=−b/(2a) when a≠0.
Check feasible endpoints and integer restrictions; the continuous optimum may be inadmissible.

recall.q: When does a quadratic's vertex give a minimum?
recall.a: When a>0.

pitfall: An unconstrained optimum may lie outside the permitted domain.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Mensuration
cue: Areas, surface areas or volumes of standard shapes appear.
theory: Match the requested quantity to its dimension: length, area or volume.
Scaling lengths by k multiplies areas by k² and volumes by k³.

recall.q: How does a cube's volume change when every edge doubles?
recall.a: It multiplies by 8.

pitfall: Surface area and volume use different units and formulas.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Remainders and cycles
cue: A large computation only asks for its remainder.
theory: Reduce intermediate values modulo the divisor and identify repetition cycles.
For a power, compute several initial remainders to establish the cycle before reducing the exponent.

recall.q: Why can multiplication be done after reducing factors modulo m?
recall.a: Congruence is preserved under multiplication.

pitfall: The exponent's remainder must be interpreted against the correct cycle and starting index.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Base representation
cue: Convert a numeral between positional number systems.
theory: In base b, digits dₖ…d₀ represent Σdᵢbⁱ, with each digit between 0 and b−1.
Repeated division by b gives integer digits from least to most significant.

recall.q: What is the value of 101 in base 2?
recall.a: 5 in decimal.

pitfall: A written digit must be smaller than the base.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Number series
cue: Find a missing or next number.
theory: Test common differences, ratios and interleaved subsequences systematically.
For an arithmetic series the differences are constant; for a geometric series the nonzero-term ratios are constant.

recall.q: What might alternating high and low terms suggest?
recall.a: Two interleaved sequences.

pitfall: Do not infer a unique rule from too few terms without checking all clues.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Number systems
cue: Parity, place value or integer categories appear.
theory: An integer is even if divisible by 2; odd+odd and even+even are even, while odd+even is odd.
Decimal divisibility by 3 or 9 follows the digit sum; divisibility by 11 follows the alternating digit sum.

recall.q: Can the product of two odd integers be even?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Zero is even, and 1 is not prime.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Number-theoretic reasoning
cue: Gcd, lcm, divisibility or prime decomposition appears.
theory: Prime factorization helps count factors and compute gcd/lcm using minimum/maximum exponents.
For positive a,b, gcd(a,b)lcm(a,b)=ab.

recall.q: In prime-factor form, how is the gcd built?
recall.a: Use the smaller exponent of each prime.

pitfall: The two-number gcd×lcm identity does not directly extend as a simple product formula for three numbers.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Numerical calculation
cue: Evaluate a numerical expression or estimate efficiently.
theory: Respect operation precedence and keep exact fractions when rounding would accumulate error.
Estimate the expected magnitude and sign before computing the final value.

recall.q: Why estimate before calculating?
recall.a: It helps detect misplaced decimals, sign errors and implausible answers.

pitfall: Round only as requested, preferably at the end.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Percentages
cue: Increase, decrease or compare a quantity relative to a base.
theory: x% of y is xy/100. Successive percentage changes multiply their factors.
Increasing by r then decreasing by the same r gives factor (1+r)(1−r)=1−r² for decimal r.

recall.q: Does +20% followed by −20% return to the original?
recall.a: No; it leaves 96% of the original.

pitfall: The base changes after the first percentage change.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Permutations versus combinations
cue: Count ordered arrangements or unordered selections.
theory: nPr=n!/(n−r)! and nCr=n!/[r!(n−r)!] for selection without repetition.
For an ordered r-slot choice with repetition allowed from n possibilities, use nʳ.

recall.q: What happens when order matters in a selection of r distinct objects?
recall.a: Each selected set has r! orders, so nPr=nCr×r!.

pitfall: Check both repetition and order before selecting a formula.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Pie charts
cue: Convert a sector's share or angle into a quantity.
theory: A sector of θ degrees represents θ/360 of the total.
A p% share corresponds to 3.6p degrees.

recall.q: What angle represents 25% of a pie?

pitfall: Charts for different totals cannot be compared using angles alone to infer absolute quantities.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Polynomial equations
cue: Use coefficients, roots or factorization of a polynomial.
theory: A root r implies (x−r) is a factor.
For ax²+bx+c, root sum is −b/a and product c/a.

recall.q: What is the remainder when polynomial f(x) is divided by x−r?
recall.a: f(r).

pitfall: The degree bound on roots counts distinct roots separately from multiplicity.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Powers and exponents
cue: Simplify repeated multiplication or compare exponential quantities.
theory: aᵐaⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ and (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ for the relevant defined domain; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ for a≠0.
When handling fractional powers over the reals, check base and root restrictions.

recall.q: What is a⁰ for a≠0?

pitfall: Do not add exponents when adding aᵐ+aⁿ.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Prime numbers
cue: Determine primality or use prime factor properties.
theory: A prime integer is greater than 1 and has exactly two positive divisors.
To test n>1 for primality, checking possible prime divisors up to √n is enough.

recall.q: Why is checking divisors only up to √n sufficient?
recall.a: A composite n has a factor pair with at least one member no larger than √n.

pitfall: 1 is neither prime nor composite.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Probability in aptitude
cue: Count random outcomes such as dice, cards or selections.
theory: For equally likely elementary outcomes, P=favourable/total.
Use complements for 'at least one'; for independent events, multiply probabilities to find their intersection.

recall.q: What is P(at least one success) in n independent trials with success probability p?

pitfall: Mutually exclusive and independent are different conditions.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Profit and loss
cue: Compare selling price with cost price.
theory: Selling price = cost price×(1+r) for profit rate r, and cost price×(1−r) for loss rate r.
Therefore recover cost by dividing the selling price by the relevant factor.

recall.q: An item sells for 110 with a 10% profit. What was its cost?

pitfall: Equal selling prices with equal percentage profit and loss do not generally cancel.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Quadratic equations
cue: An equation has highest power two.
theory: For ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0, roots are [−b±√(b²−4ac)]/(2a).
The discriminant determines real-root count: positive gives two, zero gives a repeated root, negative gives none over the reals.

recall.q: When are the two roots equal?
recall.a: When b²−4ac=0.

pitfall: A quadratic may have complex roots even when it has no real roots.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Radar charts
cue: Several attributes are shown on spokes from a centre.
theory: Read each axis's scale and value separately.
Compare the requested numerical measures directly rather than relying on the enclosed polygon's visual area.

recall.q: Why can polygon area be misleading on a radar chart?
recall.a: It depends on axis order, scaling and the arrangement of attributes.

pitfall: Do not assume every spoke uses the same scale unless shown.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Ratios and proportions
cue: Split a total or compare quantities multiplicatively.
theory: If x:y=a:b, write x=ak and y=bk; then x+y=(a+b)k.
Direct proportion keeps x/y constant; inverse proportion keeps xy constant.

recall.q: How is a total T split in ratio a:b?
recall.a: aT/(a+b) and bT/(a+b).

pitfall: Both ratio quantities must be expressed in compatible units.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Sequences and series
cue: A progression's term or total is requested.
theory: An arithmetic progression has constant differences; a geometric progression has constant ratios.
For a geometric sequence, aₙ=arⁿ⁻¹ and Sₙ=a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r) for r≠1.

recall.q: What is the distinction between a sequence and a series?
recall.a: A sequence is a list of terms; a series is their sum.

pitfall: Do not give a single term when the question asks for the cumulative sum.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Shortest routes
cue: Find the least distance through a route network or a grid.
theory: Represent allowed junctions as vertices and permitted moves as weighted edges.
For nonnegative weights, Dijkstra's method repeatedly settles the smallest tentative distance; for equal weights, BFS suffices.

recall.q: When is counting edges enough to find a shortest route?
recall.a: When every allowed edge has equal cost.

pitfall: A visually direct line may not be an allowed route.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Speed, time and distance
cue: Travel, relative motion, trains or average speed appears.
theory: Distance=speed×time; average speed=total distance/total time.
Opposite-direction relative speed adds; same-direction relative speed takes the magnitude of the difference.

recall.q: For equal distances at speeds u and v, what is average speed?
recall.a: 2uv/(u+v).

pitfall: The arithmetic mean of speeds applies to equal times, not generally equal distances.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Statistics in aptitude
cue: Summarize data using a centre or a measure of spread.
theory: Sort data for the median; use total/count for the mean and frequency for the mode.
Adding c shifts mean and median by c while leaving variance unchanged; multiplying by k scales variance by k².

recall.q: What happens to standard deviation when every value is multiplied by −3?
recall.a: It is multiplied by 3.

pitfall: Standard deviation is nonnegative and scales by the absolute factor.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Simultaneous equations
cue: Several unknown quantities satisfy multiple relationships.
theory: Translate each independent condition into an equation and solve by elimination or substitution.
Check whether equations are independent, contradictory or redundant before assuming a unique solution.

recall.q: Do two equations always determine two unknowns uniquely?
recall.a: No; they may describe the same constraint or be inconsistent.

pitfall: The number of written equations is not the same as the number of independent constraints.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Reading tables
cue: Values are arranged by rows and columns.
theory: Identify headers, units and whether entries are totals, percentages or rates.
Compute only the cells relevant to the requested comparison and check row/column totals when available.

recall.q: What is the first step before using a table entry?
recall.a: Determine exactly what its row, column and units represent.

pitfall: Do not combine percentages with different denominators as though they were raw counts.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Tabular data analysis
cue: Compare or aggregate quantities across a table.
theory: Use totals to form weighted averages or proportions; preserve the denominator attached to each value.
Missing entries may be recoverable from row sums, column sums or stated identities.

recall.q: How should two groups' success rates be combined?
recall.a: Add successes and divide by the combined number of trials.

pitfall: The largest percentage need not correspond to the largest absolute count.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Triangles
cue: Angles, similarity, side constraints or area is requested.
theory: A nondegenerate triangle needs the sum of any two side lengths to exceed the third.
Area=base×perpendicular height/2; for a right triangle, a²+b²=c² with c the hypotenuse.

recall.q: Can lengths 2,3,5 form a nondegenerate triangle?
recall.a: No; they meet equality, so the points would be collinear.

pitfall: Use the Pythagorean theorem only for a right triangle.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Venn diagrams
cue: Overlapping categories or membership counts appear.
theory: For two sets, union count = first count + second count − overlap.
For three sets, subtract all pairwise intersections and add the triple intersection once.

recall.q: Why add the triple intersection back in the three-set formula?
recall.a: After adding singles and subtracting pairs, triple members have net count zero and need one copy.

pitfall: 'Only A' excludes every overlap involving A.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Volumes
cue: Find the space occupied by a solid.
theory: A prism or cylinder has volume base area×perpendicular height; a cone or pyramid has one third of that.
Scaling every length by k scales volume by k³.

recall.q: What is a cylinder's volume?
recall.a: πr²h.

pitfall: Convert all lengths to one unit before cubing or multiplying.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Work and time
cue: Workers, pipes or machines complete a task together.
theory: If one worker completes a unit job in t time units, its rate is 1/t.
Add compatible work rates; subtract an opposing emptying or undoing rate when appropriate.

recall.q: If A needs 3 days and B needs 6, how long together at constant independent rates?

pitfall: Add rates, not completion times.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Three-dimensional structure
cue: Recognize a solid from views or count its parts.
theory: Track visible and hidden edges and keep front, side and top views consistent.
A solid's view can hide depth, so one projection may correspond to several different structures.

recall.q: Does one two-dimensional view always determine a unique solid?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Do not assume unseen blocks or edges are absent unless the diagram implies it.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Assembly of shapes
cue: Combine pieces into a target configuration.
theory: Match boundary lengths, angles and adjoining faces; consider every allowed rotation.
Check for gaps and overlaps as well as matching the outer outline.

recall.q: Why is matching only the outer outline insufficient?
recall.a: Pieces may overlap or leave internal gaps.

pitfall: A reflection is not allowed if pieces may only be rotated.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Assembling pieces
cue: Choose pieces that fit a given silhouette.
theory: Compare invariant features such as total area and corner angles before mentally moving pieces.
For a proposed fit, trace each shared boundary and confirm that no region is covered twice.

recall.q: Which easy invariant can reject an impossible assembly?
recall.a: Total area.

pitfall: Rotations preserve handedness; mirror flips change it.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Image rotations
cue: Select the result of rotating a two-dimensional figure.
theory: A rotation preserves distances and orientation of the figure's internal order; apply the same centre and angle to every feature.
Track an asymmetric landmark to distinguish 90°,180° and reflected alternatives.

recall.q: Does rotation turn a clockwise arrangement into its mirror ordering?
recall.a: No; reflection does.

pitfall: Follow the arrow's or notch's relative position, not just the overall outline.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Mirror images
cue: A figure is reflected across a mirror line.
theory: Reflection reverses the component perpendicular to the mirror and preserves distance from it.
For a vertical mirror, left and right swap; for a horizontal mirror, top and bottom swap.

recall.q: Where does a point go under reflection in a line?
recall.a: To the opposite side at the same perpendicular distance.

pitfall: A mirror image is generally not the same as a 180° rotation.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Paper folding and cuts
cue: Unfold a punched or cut folded sheet.
theory: Reverse the folds in reverse order, reflecting the current pattern across each fold line.
A mark lying on a fold may coincide with its reflected copy, so distinct-hole counts need care.

recall.q: Which fold is undone first?
recall.a: The last fold made.

pitfall: Do not blindly multiply hole count by 2 for a fold when marks coincide or lie on a boundary.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Patterns in three dimensions
cue: Mentally rotate cubes or solids with labelled faces.
theory: Under a rotation, opposite faces remain opposite and adjacent faces remain adjacent.
Track an ordered triple of faces around a corner to distinguish a true rotation from a mirror arrangement.

recall.q: Can a rigid cube rotation make opposite faces adjacent?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: Matching two visible faces alone may not determine the orientation of the third.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Patterns in two dimensions
cue: A figure changes by rotation, reflection, translation or repetition.
theory: Identify the operation between consecutive figures and apply it consistently to all features.
Separate independent changes such as shape position, shading and direction.

recall.q: What changes under translation?
recall.a: Position only; size, shape and orientation are preserved.

pitfall: Several visual features may follow different cycles.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Antonyms
cue: Choose a word with the opposite meaning in context.
theory: Determine the intended sense and part of speech before selecting an opposite.
Check whether the options oppose degree, direction or meaning, rather than merely being unrelated.

recall.q: Why does context matter for antonyms?
recall.a: A word can have several senses with different opposites.

pitfall: An unfamiliar or negative-sounding word is not necessarily an antonym.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Articles
cue: Choose a, an, the or no article.
theory: Use a/an for a nonspecific singular count noun; the choice between a and an follows sound, not spelling.
Use the for an identified or contextually specific referent, subject to established usage.

recall.q: Why is it 'an hour' but 'a university'?
recall.a: Hour begins with a vowel sound; university begins with the consonant sound /y/.

pitfall: Countability and specificity matter as well as the next letter.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Comparative forms
cue: Compare two or more quantities or people.
theory: Use the comparative for a comparison such as larger than; use the superlative to identify an extreme within a group.
Keep the compared items grammatically and logically parallel.

recall.q: What is wrong with 'more better'?
recall.a: Better is already comparative.

pitfall: Do not compare an item with a group that includes itself without a qualifier such as 'other'.
subject: General Aptitude

title: English grammar
cue: Choose a grammatically correct completion or sentence.
theory: Identify the subject, main verb and clause structure before choosing a form.
Check agreement, tense, pronoun reference and parallel structure in that order.

recall.q: In 'The list of items is long', what controls the verb?
recall.a: The singular head noun 'list'.

pitfall: A nearby noun inside a phrase need not be the subject.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Finding grammatical errors
cue: A sentence contains an agreement, tense or usage error.
theory: Read the complete sentence for meaning, then inspect each clause's subject–verb agreement and verb form.
Check that pronouns have clear antecedents and coordinated items use parallel grammatical forms.

recall.q: Why read the entire sentence before choosing an error?
recall.a: Later context can determine the tense, reference or intended structure.

pitfall: Do not mark an unusual but grammatical construction wrong merely because it sounds unfamiliar.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Locating an incorrect sentence part
cue: A sentence is split into labelled segments.
theory: Find the full subject and predicate across the segments, then locate the segment containing the actual error.
Correct the smallest part needed to restore both grammar and intended meaning.

recall.q: Can the error be found by reading each segment in isolation?
recall.a: Not reliably; relationships often cross segment boundaries.

pitfall: A segment may look incomplete alone because it belongs to a larger clause.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Choosing the appropriate word
cue: Fill a blank with the word best fitting meaning and usage.
theory: Use the sentence's logical direction and grammatical requirements to narrow the choices.
Check collocations and the precise meaning, not only whether the option is broadly related.

recall.q: What can a contrast word such as 'although' tell you?
recall.a: The clauses contrast, helping determine the blank's intended meaning.

pitfall: A grammatical word may still be semantically wrong in context.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Narrative sequencing
cue: Order events or sentences into a coherent story.
theory: Identify the setting or introductory sentence, then follow time markers, cause–effect links and references.
A pronoun or 'this event' usually requires an earlier antecedent.

recall.q: Why is a sentence starting with 'therefore' rarely a good opening?
recall.a: It normally depends on a preceding reason.

pitfall: Chronological order and explanatory order may differ; use the text's connectors.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Reading comprehension
cue: Answer from a supplied passage.
theory: Identify the main claim, supporting reasons and any qualifications.
For an inference, choose the option supported by the text without adding unstated assumptions.

recall.q: How does a main idea differ from a supporting detail?
recall.a: It states the passage's central point rather than one piece of evidence.

pitfall: Avoid answers that are true in general but unsupported by the passage.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Phrases and idioms
cue: Interpret a phrase as used in a sentence.
theory: Use context to decide whether a phrase is literal or idiomatic.
Substitute each proposed meaning and check that both the sentence's logic and tone remain consistent.

recall.q: Why can word-by-word translation fail for an idiom?
recall.a: Its conventional meaning may not equal the sum of its individual words.

pitfall: The same phrase can be literal in one context and idiomatic in another.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Prepositions
cue: Choose a relationship word such as in, on, at, to or for.
theory: Some prepositions express place or time; others are fixed by the verb, adjective or noun they follow.
Check the entire phrase's conventional usage and intended relationship.

recall.q: Why cannot a single rule settle every preposition question?
recall.a: Many constructions are conventional collocations.

pitfall: Do not choose a preposition from physical-location rules when the phrase has an abstract meaning.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Sentence ordering
cue: Arrange sentences into a coherent paragraph.
theory: Find an opening that introduces entities without unresolved references.
Link pronouns, repeated concepts, contrast markers and cause–effect transitions to form a chain.

recall.q: What is a useful clue that sentence B follows sentence A?
recall.a: B refers to an entity or event first introduced in A.

pitfall: A plausible pair is not enough; verify the whole paragraph.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Statement sufficiency
cue: Decide whether information determines an answer.
theory: Test each statement alone, then together, using only the given conditions.
Information is sufficient when every allowed case gives the same requested answer, even if all unknowns are not determined.

recall.q: Must every unknown be solved for information to be sufficient?
recall.a: No; only the requested result must be determined.

pitfall: Do not use the second statement while testing the first on its own.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Conclusions from statements
cue: Select conclusions that necessarily follow from text.
theory: Preserve quantifiers such as some, all and none when translating statements.
Test doubtful conclusions with a counterexample consistent with every premise.

recall.q: Does 'some A are B' mean 'some A are not B'?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: A statement about some members does not justify a claim about all members.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Synonyms
cue: Choose the closest meaning of a word in context.
theory: Identify the word's sense, tone and grammatical role in the sentence.
Prefer the closest contextual meaning, not just a loose association.

recall.q: Can two dictionary synonyms always replace each other?
recall.a: No; register, collocation and context may differ.

pitfall: Related meaning is weaker than equivalent meaning in the specific sentence.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Verb tenses
cue: Events occur at different times or relative to another event.
theory: Locate the time reference, then distinguish ongoing, completed and repeated actions.
Perfect forms relate an earlier event to a later reference point; continuous forms emphasize an action in progress.

recall.q: What does past perfect typically mark relative to another past event?
recall.a: An event completed earlier than that past reference point.

pitfall: Do not shift tense without a change in time reference or intended meaning.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Verbal reasoning
cue: Assess an argument, inference, assumption or relationship in prose.
theory: Separate premises from the conclusion and identify the link the argument depends on.
An assumption is an unstated premise needed for the reasoning; a conclusion is what the argument attempts to establish.

recall.q: How can you test a proposed necessary assumption?
recall.a: Consider whether denying it undermines the argument's required reasoning.

pitfall: An emotionally persuasive statement need not be logically relevant.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Word meanings
cue: Choose a definition or infer meaning from surrounding text.
theory: Use nearby explanations, contrasts and examples to constrain meaning.
Check whether the option matches the word's part of speech and strength.

recall.q: What clue does 'unlike' often provide?
recall.a: A contrast that helps infer the unknown word's meaning.

pitfall: A familiar meaning may not be the meaning used in the passage.
subject: General Aptitude

title: Word pairs and relationships
cue: Choose a pair whose relationship matches a model.
theory: Describe the model pair with a short directional phrase, then apply the same phrase to each candidate.
Match level and category: cause→effect, tool→purpose, part→whole or synonym/antonym.

recall.q: Why is the direction of a word-pair relation important?
recall.a: Cause→effect is not the same relation as effect→cause.

pitfall: A pair sharing the same topic can still express a different relationship.
subject: General Aptitude
